title: Beta Blockers and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Drink?
excerpt: Can you drink on a beta blocker? How alcohol and beta blockers like metoprolol, propranolol, carvedilol, and atenolol interact, how much is too much, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on beta blockers? How alcohol interacts with metoprolol, propranolol, carvedilol, and atenolol, safe limits, and warning signs to watch.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most people taking a beta blocker for blood pressure or a heart condition, an occasional drink with a meal is often fine, and many doctors allow it. The risk comes from the way the two add together. Both alcohol and beta blockers can lower your blood pressure, and the beta blocker also stops your heart from speeding up to compensate. The result can be dizziness, light-headedness, or fainting, especially when you stand up quickly, drink more than usual, or drink on an empty stomach. Regular heavy drinking also raises blood pressure over time and works against the medicine you're taking to lower it.

**The quick rules:** Never skip or stop a beta blocker dose so you can drink. Stopping suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound in heart rate and blood pressure. Keep drinks light (most heart and blood pressure guidance points to no more than one drink a day for women and two for men, and less is better), eat first, stand up slowly, and pay attention to how you feel the first few times you drink after starting a new beta blocker or changing the dose. If you take carvedilol extended-release (Coreg CR), follow the label's specific instruction about keeping alcohol away from your dose. If you have diabetes, know that a beta blocker can hide some of the warning signs of low blood sugar, and alcohol makes low blood sugar more likely.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains how beta blockers and alcohol interact in general terms. It is not a substitute for the doctor or pharmacist who knows your diagnosis, dose, and other medicines, so **talk to your doctor before combining alcohol with any beta blocker.** **Get medical help right away if** you faint or nearly faint, have chest pain or pressure, feel your heart beating very slowly, irregularly, or very fast, become short of breath, feel confused, or have signs of very low blood sugar such as sweating, shakiness, or confusion. In an emergency, call 911 (or your local emergency number).

## What Beta Blockers Do (in Plain Words)

Beta blockers are a family of prescription medicines that block the effect of adrenaline (also called epinephrine) and related stress hormones on the heart and blood vessels. Adrenaline normally makes your heart beat faster and harder. When a beta blocker sits on those "beta" receptors, your heart beats more slowly and with less force, and your blood pressure comes down.

Doctors prescribe them for a long list of reasons:

- **High blood pressure**, although they're no longer the usual first choice for uncomplicated hypertension
- **After a heart attack**, to protect the heart
- **Heart failure** (certain beta blockers specifically)
- **Angina** (chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart)
- **Irregular heart rhythms**, including atrial fibrillation and some fast heart rates
- **Migraine prevention**
- **Essential tremor**
- **Performance anxiety**, such as stage fright before a speech (this is an off-label use, mostly of propranolol)
- **Overactive thyroid symptoms**, to calm a racing heart while the thyroid is treated

The most common beta blockers you'll see on a pill bottle include **metoprolol** (Lopressor, Toprol-XL), **propranolol** (Inderal, Inderal LA), **atenolol** (Tenormin), **carvedilol** (Coreg, Coreg CR), **bisoprolol**, **nebivolol** (Bystolic), **labetalol**, and **nadolol**. They share the same basic action, but they differ in ways that matter when alcohol enters the picture, which we'll cover below.

## Why Beta Blockers and Alcohol Interact: The Real Mechanism

There's no single chemical reaction between a beta blocker and alcohol. Instead, they push on the same parts of your circulation in ways that add up. There are four main pieces.

### 1. Both lower blood pressure, and the effects stack

Alcohol relaxes and widens blood vessels in the hours after you drink. That's part of why your face may flush and why some people feel warm after a glass of wine. Wider vessels mean lower blood pressure in the short term. A beta blocker is already lowering your blood pressure. Put the two together and pressure can dip further than either would cause alone.

For most people this shows up as **orthostatic hypotension**, which means a drop in blood pressure when you go from lying or sitting to standing. You get up from the table or out of bed, the room goes grey or spins for a few seconds, and you may need to grab something. In a minority of people, especially older adults, people on several blood pressure medicines, or anyone who's dehydrated, it can lead to fainting and falls.

### 2. The beta blocker blocks your body's usual rescue

When blood pressure drops, your body normally fixes it in a second or two by speeding up your heart. That reflex depends on adrenaline acting on beta receptors, which is exactly what your medicine blocks. So the usual safety net is weaker. Your heart can't speed up as much to push blood back up to your brain when you stand, and the dizziness lasts longer or hits harder.

This is the part of the interaction that's easy to miss. It isn't only that two things lower blood pressure. It's that one of them also switches off the backup system.

### 3. Alcohol and the medicine can both make you drowsy and slow

Tiredness and fatigue are common side effects of beta blockers, particularly in the first weeks of treatment. Some, such as propranolol and metoprolol, pass into the brain more easily and can cause vivid dreams, low energy, or a flat mood in some people. Alcohol is a sedative. Together they can make you sleepier, slower to react, and more unsteady than you'd expect from the number of drinks you've had. Be careful about driving, and don't assume your usual tolerance still applies.

### 4. Regular drinking works against the medicine over time

The short-term effect of a drink is to lower blood pressure. The long-term effect of regular, heavier drinking is the opposite: it **raises** blood pressure and is one of the more common reversible causes of hypertension. Heavy drinking also raises the risk of irregular heart rhythms, especially atrial fibrillation, and over many years can weaken the heart muscle itself. If you're taking a beta blocker for any of these problems, frequent heavy drinking undercuts the reason you're on it. Our guide to [alcohol and blood pressure](/never-hungover/alcohol-hypertension-blood-pressure-management-2025) goes deeper on that long-term picture.

## What the Labels and Official Guidance Say

Prescribing information for beta blockers doesn't usually carry a blanket ban on alcohol. What it does carry, and what pharmacists commonly put on the bottle sticker, is a warning that alcohol can add to dizziness and drowsiness, plus a few drug-specific instructions:

- **Carvedilol extended-release (Coreg CR):** The US label warns that alcohol can make the capsule release its medicine faster than it should. It tells patients not to drink alcohol, or take medicines that contain alcohol, for about two hours before or after a dose. The regular carvedilol tablet (Coreg) doesn't carry that specific instruction, but the general dizziness caution still applies.
- **Propranolol:** Prescribing information notes that alcohol can change propranolol blood levels when the two are used together. In practice this means the effect of a given dose can be less predictable on a night you're drinking.
- **Several beta blockers, including metoprolol, propranolol, and atenolol:** Their US labels carry a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest kind, about stopping the drug abruptly in people with coronary artery disease. That warning is the reason you should never skip doses to make room for a night out.

On how much to drink at all, heart and blood pressure guidelines from groups such as the American Heart Association advise people with high blood pressure who drink to keep it to no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women. Newer guidance from several health bodies leans toward "less is better" and notes that no amount of alcohol is risk-free. Your own doctor may set a lower limit depending on why you take the medicine.

## How Much Can You Drink on a Beta Blocker?

There isn't a single safe number that applies to everyone, because it depends on which beta blocker you take, the dose, why you take it, your age, and what else you're on. That said, these points hold for most people:

- **One standard drink with food** is something many doctors are comfortable with for patients whose blood pressure and heart rhythm are stable. A standard drink in the US is about 12 ounces of regular beer, 5 ounces of wine, or 1.5 ounces of spirits.
- **Two drinks** is the upper end of what blood pressure guidelines allow for men, and many people on beta blockers feel noticeably more light-headed at that level than they used to.
- **Binge drinking** (roughly four or more drinks for women or five or more for men on one occasion) is where the real trouble starts: big blood pressure swings, dehydration, a higher chance of a heart rhythm problem, and a rough next morning with a heart that can't respond normally.

If you've just started a beta blocker or your dose was recently increased, give yourself a couple of weeks before drinking much, and test the waters with a single drink at home rather than at a party far from home. That first night tells you a lot about how your body handles the combination.

## Never Skip a Dose to Drink

This is the single most important point on this page, and it's the mistake people make most often. It seems sensible: "I'll skip my evening pill tonight so it doesn't clash with the wine." With beta blockers, that logic is backwards.

When you take a beta blocker every day, your body adapts by becoming more sensitive to adrenaline. If the medicine suddenly disappears, that extra sensitivity is left with nothing holding it back. Heart rate and blood pressure can rebound above where they were before treatment. In people with heart disease this rebound has been linked to worsening chest pain, heart attacks, and dangerous rhythms, which is why several beta blockers carry the boxed warning mentioned above.

A single missed dose is unlikely to cause a crisis in most people, but deliberately skipping doses on drinking nights, week after week, is the kind of on-off pattern doctors want to avoid. Take your medicine as prescribed and adjust the drinking, not the dose. If you're worried about the combination, ask your doctor whether the timing of your dose can be moved. That's a much safer conversation than skipping pills on your own.

## Differences Between Common Beta Blockers

Beta blockers aren't all the same, and a few differences matter for drinking.

| Beta blocker | Common brand names | What to know with alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Metoprolol | Lopressor (tartrate), Toprol-XL (succinate) | Very widely prescribed. Can cause tiredness and vivid dreams. Don't crush or chew the extended-release tablets. Never stop suddenly. |
| Propranolol | Inderal, Inderal LA | Often used for anxiety, migraine, and tremor. Passes into the brain readily, so drowsiness with alcohol is more likely. Label notes alcohol can change its blood levels. |
| Atenolol | Tenormin | Doesn't enter the brain as much, so may cause less drowsiness. Cleared by the kidneys. Still adds to blood pressure lowering and can mask low blood sugar. |
| Carvedilol | Coreg, Coreg CR | Also blocks alpha receptors, which widens blood vessels, so dizziness on standing is more common. Coreg CR label says to keep alcohol about two hours away from your dose. |
| Bisoprolol | Generic, sometimes combined with a water pill | Similar cautions to metoprolol. Combination pills add a diuretic, which can make dehydration from drinking worse. |
| Nebivolol | Bystolic | Also relaxes blood vessels. Same dizziness and blood pressure cautions. |
| Labetalol | Generic | Blocks alpha and beta receptors, so drops in blood pressure on standing are a known side effect even without alcohol. |

The pattern: beta blockers that also widen blood vessels (carvedilol, labetalol, nebivolol) and combination pills that include a water pill are the ones where dizziness from alcohol tends to be most noticeable. Beta blockers that reach the brain more easily (propranolol, metoprolol) are the ones more likely to add to alcohol's drowsiness.

### Metoprolol and alcohol

Metoprolol is one of the most prescribed heart medicines in the US. It comes in two forms: metoprolol tartrate (usually taken twice a day) and metoprolol succinate, an extended-release version taken once a day. Alcohol doesn't have a special interaction with either beyond the general ones: more dizziness, more drowsiness, and a weaker heart-rate response if your blood pressure dips. The big rule is the one above. Metoprolol carries the boxed warning about stopping suddenly, so don't skip doses around drinking.

### Propranolol and alcohol, including for performance anxiety

We cover this one in depth in our [propranolol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/propranolol-and-alcohol). The short version:

A lot of people searching this topic take a low dose of propranolol before a wedding speech, presentation, or interview, and then wonder about the champagne afterwards. A single low dose taken for performance anxiety is a different situation from daily treatment for heart disease, but the same mechanics apply: alcohol on top of propranolol can make you more light-headed and tired than usual, and the effect is stronger if you haven't eaten.

If that's you, a few practical points: have your first drink with food, not on an empty stomach right after the event; alternate with water; and don't use alcohol as a second anxiety treatment on top of the pill. Ask the doctor who prescribed it how long after your dose you should wait. If you notice that you're relying on drinks to get through social situations, our guide to [hangxiety and the anxiety-alcohol cycle](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) is worth a read.

### Carvedilol and alcohol

Carvedilol is often prescribed for heart failure and after a heart attack. Because it also widens blood vessels, it's more likely than many beta blockers to cause dizziness when you stand up, and alcohol adds to that. The extended-release capsule (Coreg CR) has the specific label instruction to avoid alcohol for about two hours before and after a dose, because alcohol can speed up how quickly the capsule releases the drug. People with heart failure also often have fluid and salt limits, and drinking can complicate both, so this is one to discuss directly with your cardiologist.

### Atenolol and alcohol

Atenolol is less likely to cause drowsiness because it doesn't cross into the brain as much. It's cleared by the kidneys, so its levels aren't much affected by how hard your liver is working on alcohol. It still lowers blood pressure, still blunts your heart's ability to speed up, and still masks some low blood sugar warning signs, so the general advice is the same.

## Beta Blockers, Alcohol, and Low Blood Sugar

This deserves its own section because it's a real safety issue for people with diabetes, and it's often overlooked.

Alcohol makes low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) more likely, because while your liver is busy processing alcohol it releases less stored sugar into the blood. The risk is highest when you drink without eating and for several hours afterwards, including overnight. It's a particular concern for anyone who takes insulin or a sulfonylurea such as glipizide or glyburide.

Beta blockers add a second problem. Many of the early warning signs of low blood sugar, such as a pounding or racing heart, shakiness, and anxiety, are driven by adrenaline. A beta blocker can blunt or hide those signals. Sweating usually still happens, so it can be one of the few early clues left.

Put together: alcohol makes a low more likely, and the beta blocker makes it harder to notice. If you have diabetes and take a beta blocker:

- Eat carbohydrates when you drink, and don't drink on an empty stomach.
- Check your blood sugar before bed after drinking, and consider a snack.
- Make sure the people you're with know the signs of low blood sugar, including confusion that can look like drunkenness.
- Talk to your doctor about your personal targets and plan. Our guide to [alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025) covers this in more detail.

## The Morning After: Hangovers on Beta Blockers

People on beta blockers sometimes describe hangovers that feel different. That makes sense given how the medicine works.

- **A racing heart may be muted.** A fast heartbeat the morning after drinking is common, and it's partly driven by adrenaline and dehydration. A beta blocker can dampen it. That can feel like a relief, but it also means a rapid heartbeat that breaks through the medicine is worth taking seriously. Our page on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains the usual causes and when to worry.
- **Dizziness may be worse.** Dehydration lowers blood pressure further, and your heart can't compensate as easily. Drink water before bed and again in the morning, and get up slowly.
- **Fatigue may be heavier.** Poor sleep after alcohol plus medicine-related tiredness can leave you flatter than usual.
- **Some painkillers need thought.** Ibuprofen and naproxen can raise blood pressure and blunt the effect of blood pressure medicines when used regularly, and they're hard on the stomach after drinking. An occasional dose is usually fine for many people, but if you take a beta blocker for blood pressure or heart failure, check with your pharmacist about which pain reliever suits you. For acetaminophen, read our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) first, because it has its own liver cautions.

## Holiday Heart: Why Binges Are the Real Risk

Doctors use the phrase "holiday heart syndrome" for episodes of irregular heartbeat, most often atrial fibrillation, that show up after a bout of heavy drinking, classically around holidays and weekends. It can happen in people with no known heart disease, and it's more likely in people who already have a rhythm problem.

Many people take beta blockers precisely to control heart rate in atrial fibrillation or to prevent other rhythm problems. A binge can trigger an episode that breaks through the medicine. If you notice a fluttering, irregular, or pounding heartbeat after a night of drinking that doesn't settle within a short time, or it comes with chest pain, shortness of breath, or fainting, get checked. Don't sleep it off.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

Most people who have a drink or two on a beta blocker feel nothing worse than a bit of extra light-headedness. These signs are different and need medical attention.

**Call 911 or go to an emergency department if you have:**

- Fainting, or nearly fainting more than once
- Chest pain, pressure, or tightness
- A heartbeat that's very slow (especially with dizziness or confusion), very fast, or irregular and not settling
- Shortness of breath or wheezing (beta blockers can tighten airways in some people with asthma)
- Confusion, slurred speech, or trouble staying awake beyond what you'd expect from what you drank
- Signs of severe low blood sugar if you have diabetes

**Call your doctor or pharmacist soon if:**

- You get dizzy every time you drink, even with one drink
- You've fallen or nearly fallen after drinking
- You've started skipping doses around drinking and want a safer plan
- Your home blood pressure readings are running higher than your target on days after drinking

**If you drink heavily every day:** don't stop suddenly on your own. Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous, with shaking, sweating, a racing heart, seizures, or confusion. A beta blocker can hide some of those warning signs, such as tremor and a fast heart rate, so withdrawal can be more serious than it looks. Talk to a doctor before cutting back, so it can be done safely.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're more likely to run into trouble with alcohol on a beta blocker if you:

- Are older, or have had falls before
- Take more than one blood pressure medicine, or a beta blocker combined with a water pill
- Have heart failure, a recent heart attack, or a rhythm problem such as atrial fibrillation
- Have diabetes, especially if you take insulin or a sulfonylurea
- Have asthma or chronic lung disease
- Also take other medicines that cause drowsiness, such as sleep aids, some antihistamines, opioids, or anxiety medicines
- Have just started a beta blocker or changed your dose

If any of these apply, it's worth asking your doctor directly whether you should drink at all and, if so, how much.

## Smart Habits If You Do Drink

If your doctor is comfortable with you drinking on your beta blocker, these habits make it a lot smoother:

1. **Keep taking your medicine as prescribed.** Don't skip or delay doses for a night out.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows alcohol absorption and helps keep blood sugar steady.
3. **Set a limit before you start.** One drink, or two at most, is a sensible ceiling for most people on these medicines.
4. **Alternate with water.** Dehydration worsens dizziness and next-day symptoms.
5. **Stand up slowly.** Sit on the edge of the bed or chair for a moment before getting up, especially at night.
6. **Don't drive.** Even if you'd normally feel fine after a drink, the combination can slow you down more than you expect.
7. **Watch the binge pattern.** Steady light drinking is far easier on a treated heart than nothing all week and five drinks on Saturday.
8. **Check your blood pressure at home** if you have a cuff, especially the morning after drinking, and share the readings with your doctor.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

People who read this site are often interested in DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. It's worth being clear about what it does and doesn't do here.

There is no good evidence that DHM changes how beta blockers work, and it has not been studied alongside them in people. It does not prevent the blood pressure drop, the dizziness, or the low blood sugar risk described above, and it doesn't make a binge any safer for your heart. Most DHM research comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. If you take a beta blocker and want to try any supplement, including DHM, mention it to your doctor or pharmacist first so they can check it against your full medication list. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.

If your doctor is fine with it and you drink lightly, some people use DHM as part of a sensible routine alongside food, water, and pacing. A widely available option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains typical amounts and timing. It's a minor extra, not a safety measure. The steps that genuinely protect you on a beta blocker are drinking less, eating, staying hydrated, and taking your medicine as prescribed.

## The Bottom Line

Beta blockers and alcohol both lower blood pressure, and the beta blocker also stops your heart from speeding up to make up for it. That's why the main risk is dizziness and fainting, particularly when you stand up, drink more than usual, or haven't eaten. Regular heavy drinking also raises blood pressure and the risk of rhythm problems, which works against the reason you're on the medicine. Light drinking with food is often acceptable, but only your doctor can say what's right for your heart and your dose. Never skip a dose to drink, follow any drug-specific instructions on your label (such as the two-hour rule for Coreg CR), and if you have diabetes, plan for the fact that low blood sugar may be harder to notice. For a broader view of drinking and heart health, see our [cardiovascular guide](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-heart-health-complete-cardiovascular-guide-2025).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking beta blockers?**

Many people can have an occasional drink with food, and many doctors allow it for patients whose blood pressure and heart rhythm are stable. The main risk is that alcohol and the beta blocker together lower blood pressure, while the medicine also stops your heart from speeding up to compensate, which can cause dizziness or fainting. Ask your doctor what limit is right for your condition and dose.

**How much alcohol is safe on a beta blocker?**

There is no single number for everyone. Blood pressure guidance from groups such as the American Heart Association says people with high blood pressure who drink should keep it to no more than two drinks a day for men and one for women, and less is better. Avoid binge drinking entirely, eat when you drink, and let your doctor set your personal limit.

**Should I skip my beta blocker if I'm going to drink?**

No. Several beta blockers, including metoprolol, propranolol, and atenolol, carry a boxed warning about stopping suddenly, because heart rate and blood pressure can rebound and, in people with heart disease, trigger chest pain or a heart attack. Keep taking your medicine as prescribed and cut back on the drinking instead. If you're worried about timing, ask your doctor whether your dose time can be moved.

**Can I drink alcohol with metoprolol?**

Metoprolol has no special interaction with alcohol beyond the general ones: more dizziness, more drowsiness, and a weaker heart-rate response if your blood pressure drops. Light drinking with food is often acceptable, but check with your doctor, never skip doses to drink, and don't crush or chew the extended-release tablets.

**Is it OK to drink after taking propranolol for anxiety?**

A single low dose for performance anxiety is different from daily heart treatment, but alcohol can still make you more light-headed and tired, especially on an empty stomach. Eat first, keep it to a drink or two, alternate with water, and ask the prescriber how long to wait after your dose. Propranolol's prescribing information also notes that alcohol can change its blood levels.

**Why does carvedilol extended-release have a two-hour alcohol rule?**

The US label for Coreg CR warns that alcohol can make the capsule release its medicine faster than intended. It tells patients not to drink alcohol, or take medicines containing alcohol, for about two hours before or after a dose. Regular carvedilol tablets don't carry that specific instruction, but the general dizziness caution still applies.

**Do beta blockers hide the signs of low blood sugar after drinking?**

They can. A racing heart, shakiness, and anxiety are early warning signs of low blood sugar driven by adrenaline, and beta blockers can blunt them. Sweating usually still occurs. Alcohol also makes low blood sugar more likely, especially without food and overnight. If you have diabetes, eat when you drink, check your blood sugar before bed, and talk to your doctor about a plan.

**Does DHM interact with beta blockers?**

DHM has not been studied alongside beta blockers in people, and there is no good evidence that it changes how they work or that it prevents the blood pressure drop or dizziness from drinking. Mention any supplement, including DHM, to your doctor or pharmacist before combining it with a beta blocker.
